cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 1(a): Five riparian States of the river Sella — Valdor, Kastria, Lumen, Brisa and Monteno — negotiate the Sella Basin Water Convention (SBWC), which obliges the parties to prevent pollution of the river. On 4 March 2025 a diplomatic conference in Valdor's capital adopted the text; Article 25(1) provides that the Convention 'shall be subject to ratification'. On the same day the SBWC was signed for Valdor by its Foreign Minister, for Kastria by its Prime Minister, for Lumen by its Minister of the Environment and for Brisa by its ambassador accredited to Valdor; neither the Minister of the Environment nor the ambassador produced full powers. Monteno signed on 11 March 2025 through a Deputy Foreign Minister holding full powers. Could these persons validly sign the SBWC on behalf of their States, and what is the legal effect of their signatures? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Valdor's Foreign Minister, Kastria's Prime Minister and Monteno's Deputy Foreign Minister (full powers) signed validly; Lumen's minister and Brisa's ambassador needed full powers, so their signatures have no legal effect unless full powers were dispensed with or the State later confirms them (Arts 7–8 VCLT); a signature subject to ratification is not consent to be bound.
• Rule: full powers are required (Art 7(1)(a)) unless the States intended to dispense with them (Art 7(1)(b)). Ex officio: Heads of State, Heads of Government and Foreign Ministers for all acts (Art 7(2)(a)); ambassadors and conference delegates only to adopt the text — ambassadors only of a treaty between the accrediting and the receiving State (Art 7(2)(b)–(c)).
• Application: Valdor and Kastria → Art 7(2)(a); Monteno → full powers. Lumen's minister is not one of the 'big three'; Brisa's ambassador signs (not merely adopts) a multilateral convention → full powers needed; otherwise no legal effect unless afterwards confirmed by the State (Art 8), e.g. by ratification.
• Effect: signature authenticates the text (Art 10(b)) but is not consent to be bound, because the SBWC requires ratification (Art 14(1)(a)); the signatory must refrain from acts that would defeat the object and purpose until it makes clear that it will not become a party (Art 18(a)).
Memorise: Art 7(2)(a) big three = all acts · ambassador / delegate = adoption of the text only · others: full powers (7(1)(a)) or dispensation (7(1)(b)) · else no effect unless confirmed (Art 8) · signature = Art 10(b) + Art 18(a), not consent (Art 14).

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 1(b): Five riparian States of the river Sella — Valdor, Kastria, Lumen, Brisa and Monteno — adopted and signed the Sella Basin Water Convention (SBWC) in March 2025; Valdor is the depositary. Article 25 SBWC reads: '1. This Convention shall be subject to ratification. It shall be open for accession by any other State. 2. It shall enter into force on the ninetieth day after the date of deposit of the third instrument of ratification or accession. 3. For each State ratifying or acceding after the deposit of the third instrument, the Convention shall enter into force on the thirtieth day after the deposit by such State of its instrument.' Kastria deposited its instrument of ratification on 14.05.2025 and Valdor on 28.11.2025. Lumen's President signed Lumen's instrument of ratification on 20.10.2025, but it was deposited only on 03.12.2025. Monteno deposited its instrument of ratification on 10.02.2026. In January 2026 Brisa's new government notified the depositary that Brisa would not ratify. When did the SBWC enter into force? When did it enter into force for Valdor, Monteno and Brisa? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Objective entry into force on 03.03.2026, which is also the date for Valdor (and for Kastria and Lumen); for Monteno on 12.03.2026; for Brisa never.
• Rule: a treaty enters into force as it provides (Art 24(1) VCLT), for a State consenting later on the date the treaty provides for it (Art 24(3)). Consent by ratification is established on deposit (Art 16(b)), and Art 25(2) itself counts deposits — the date on which Lumen's President signed the instrument is irrelevant.
• Third deposit: Kastria 14.05.2025, Valdor 28.11.2025, Lumen 03.12.2025. 90th day after 03.12.2025: 28 days of December (4–31) + 31 of January + 28 of February 2026 (no leap year) = 87, + 3 days of March → 03.03.2026 = objective entry into force.
• Valdor, Kastria and Lumen deposited up to and including the third instrument → bound from 03.03.2026.
• Monteno deposited after the third instrument → Art 25(3): 30th day after 10.02.2026 = 18 days of February (11–28) + 12 of March → 12.03.2026. (Had that day fallen before 03.03.2026, Monteno would have had to wait for the objective date: no subjective before the objective entry into force.)
• Brisa: a mere signatory, never a party (Art 2(1)(g)); its Art 18(a) duty ended with its notification that it would not ratify.
• Trap: counting the date on which Lumen's instrument was signed (20.10.2025) would make Valdor's deposit the third and give 26.02.2026 — wrong.
Memorise: count DEPOSITS, not ratification dates (Art 16(b)) · 03.12.2025 + 90 days = 03.03.2026 · later joiners: own deposit + 30 days (Monteno 12.03.2026) · never before the objective date · signatory ≠ party.

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 1(c): The Sella Basin Water Convention (SBWC) has been in force between the riparian States Valdor, Kastria, Lumen and Monteno since March 2026 and is open for accession by any State; Valdor is the depositary. Article 14 SBWC provides for compulsory arbitration of disputes between the parties; Article 26 provides: 'No reservations may be made to Articles 1 to 8.' On 25.08.2026 Ostrel, a downstream State that had not taken part in the negotiations, deposits an instrument of accession containing an 'interpretative declaration': 'Ostrel understands Article 14 as not applying to disputes to which Ostrel is a party.' The depositary notifies the parties on 01.09.2026. Kastria accepts the declaration in writing on 15.09.2026; Valdor objects in writing on 10.11.2026 without further comment; Monteno objects in writing on 20.11.2026 and declares that the SBWC shall not enter into force between itself and Ostrel; Lumen does not react. Is Ostrel's declaration a reservation, and is it admissible? What treaty relations exist between Ostrel and each of the four parties? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: It is a reservation despite its label, and an admissible one; Ostrel–Kastria (and Ostrel–Lumen once twelve months of silence have run): SBWC in force without Art 14, reciprocally; Ostrel–Valdor: in force, but Art 14 does not apply between them; Ostrel–Monteno: no treaty relations.
• Qualification: a unilateral statement, however phrased or named, made on signing, ratifying or acceding, by which a State purports to exclude or modify the legal effect of certain provisions for itself (Art 2(1)(d) VCLT). Ostrel does not interpret Art 14, it excludes it → reservation (Belilos v Switzerland, ECtHR 1988).
• Admissibility: made on accession, in writing (Arts 19, 23(1)). Art 26 bans reservations only to Arts 1–8 (Art 19(a)); other reservations are not thereby 'expressly authorized' (Art 20(1)) and must pass Art 19(c). Excluding compulsory arbitration leaves the anti-pollution duties intact → compatible with the object and purpose (cf. Armed Activities (DRC v Rwanda), ICJ 2006). Acceptance by all (Art 20(2)) is not needed: the Convention is open to any State and itself envisages reservations.
• Kastria: express acceptance (Art 20(4)(a)), which also makes Ostrel's accession effective (Art 20(4)(c)); Art 14 excluded in both directions (Art 21(1)).
• Valdor: simple objection within twelve months (Art 20(5)) → treaty in force, but Art 14 does not apply between them to the extent of the reservation (Arts 20(4)(b), 21(3)).
• Monteno: qualified objection (contrary intention definitely expressed) → no treaty relations (Art 20(4)(b)).
• Lumen: no objection by 01.09.2027 (twelve months after notification) → deemed acceptance (Art 20(5)), then as Kastria. Relations among the four parties are unaffected (Art 21(2)).
Memorise: 'however phrased or named' (Art 2(1)(d), Belilos) · partial ban (19(a)) → others still 19(c) · dispute-clause reservation = compatible (DRC v Rwanda 2006) · one acceptance makes the accession effective (20(4)(c)) · acceptance / 12 months' silence → 21(1) · simple objection → 21(3) · qualified → none (20(4)(b)).

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 1(d): Article 5(1) of the Sella Basin Water Convention (SBWC), in force between the Sella riparian States, obliges each party 'to prevent any discharge of untreated industrial wastewater into the Sella and its tributaries'. The preamble states that the parties are 'determined to protect the waters of the Sella basin against pollution'. In 2027 Kastria authorises a chemical plant to inject untreated wastewater into an underground aquifer which feeds the Sella. Ostrel, a downstream party which acceded in 2026 without having taken part in the negotiations, protests. Kastria replies: 'The conference records show that Lumen's proposal to add the words “and connected groundwater” was withdrawn. These records are decisive: Article 5 does not cover aquifers.' Do you agree with Kastria? Give reasons. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — conference records are travaux préparatoires, only a supplementary means of interpretation (Art 32 VCLT); Art 31 comes first and points to covering discharges that reach the Sella through an aquifer, and a withdrawn proposal cannot override that result, least of all against Ostrel.
• Art 31: good faith, ordinary meaning of the terms in their context (including the preamble, Art 31(2)) and in the light of the object and purpose. Wastewater injected into an aquifer that feeds the river reaches the Sella indirectly; the preamble ('protect the waters of the Sella basin') and effet utile support covering it — otherwise Art 5 could be evaded at will.
• Art 32: travaux may confirm the Art 31 result, and determine the meaning only if Art 31 leaves it ambiguous or obscure or leads to a manifestly absurd or unreasonable result — never 'decisive' on their own. A withdrawn proposal is weak evidence: it may have been withdrawn as superfluous, and at most it shows that groundwater as such is not protected — not that discharges reaching the river through it are allowed.
• Ostrel did not take part in the negotiations and relied on the text; travaux carry less weight against acceding States (River Oder Commission, PCIJ 1929).
Memorise: Art 31 first (good faith + text + context incl. preamble + object and purpose) · Art 32 travaux = confirm, or determine only if ambiguous/absurd · withdrawn proposal = weak · acceding States (River Oder 1929).

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 2(a): The United Nations runs a regional humanitarian logistics hub, which is part of the UN Secretariat, in the capital of State Feronia. Feronia is a UN member and a party to the 1946 Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the United Nations (General Convention). In 2026 the hub terminates its contract with the Feronian trucking company TransCargo for alleged poor performance. TransCargo sues the United Nations before the Commercial Court of Feronia for EUR 2 million in damages, arguing that a commercial transport contract has nothing to do with the UN's sovereign tasks. Will the Feronian court hear the case? Explain the legal basis and the rationale of the UN's immunity, and what TransCargo can do instead. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — the UN enjoys immunity from every form of legal process unless it expressly waives it in the particular case (Art 105(1) UN Charter; Section 2 General Convention), and this also covers commercial contracts; TransCargo must use the settlement procedure the UN is obliged to provide, in practice arbitration (Section 29(a)).
• Legal basis: Art 105(1) Charter — the UN enjoys in the territory of each member the privileges and immunities necessary for the fulfilment of its purposes; Section 2 — the UN, its property and assets are immune from every form of legal process unless it has expressly waived immunity in a particular case, and no waiver extends to execution. Feronia is bound as member and as party; the hub has no separate legal personality, so the claim is against the UN itself.
• Rationale: functional necessity — the independence of the Organization; no member or host State may control its work through its own courts.
• No commercial exception: unlike restrictive State immunity (none for acta iure gestionis such as commercial contracts), the UN's immunity is functional in rationale but absolute in practice → TransCargo's argument fails; without an express waiver the court must decline jurisdiction.
• Alternative: Section 29(a) obliges the UN to provide appropriate modes of settlement for contractual and other private-law disputes; UN contracts provide for amicable settlement and then arbitration under the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules. Such alternative means are also why the immunity is compatible with access to court (Art 6 ECHR; Waite and Kennedy v Germany, ECtHR 1999).
Memorise: Art 105(1) Charter + Section 2 = immunity from every form of legal process · waiver only express, never for execution · absolute in practice (commercial acts too) ≠ restrictive State immunity · Section 29(a) → arbitration · Waite and Kennedy 1999.

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 2(b): The United Nations runs a humanitarian logistics hub, part of the UN Secretariat, in State Feronia, a UN member and party to the 1946 Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the United Nations. Mr Rusk, a Feronian national, is a procurement officer (UN staff member) at the hub. In an internal evaluation report he wrote that managers of the trucking company TransCargo had bribed Feronian customs officials; the report was later leaked to the press. TransCargo's CEO sues Rusk for defamation before a Feronian court. The UN Secretary-General informs the court that Rusk wrote the report in his official capacity and that his immunity is maintained. The court replies that, as a Feronian citizen, Rusk is fully subject to Feronian law, and that it alone decides whether he acted officially. Assess the court's position. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The court is wrong on both points: Rusk enjoys functional immunity for words written in his official capacity, also against his own State, and the Secretary-General's finding that he acted officially must be given the greatest weight and can be set aside only for the most compelling reasons (Cumaraswamy AO 1999).
• Rule: UN officials are immune from legal process in respect of words spoken or written and all acts performed in their official capacity (Art 105(2) Charter; Section 18(a) General Convention). The immunity protects the independence of the Organization, not the person.
• Official act: an evaluation report on a contractor, written by a procurement officer as part of his duties, is official; the leak by someone else does not turn it into a private statement.
• Nationality: the Convention makes no exception for nationals — unlike diplomats, UN officials are protected also against their State of nationality (cf. Mazilu AO 1989 and Cumaraswamy, both on experts on mission — Cumaraswamy, a Malaysian, was sued before Malaysian courts). 'As a Feronian citizen' is irrelevant.
• Who decides: only the Secretary-General can waive an official's immunity (Section 20), and he maintains it. His finding on the official character creates a presumption that national courts must give the greatest weight; immunity is a preliminary question to be decided expeditiously in limine litis (Cumaraswamy).
• Consequence: if the court proceeds, Feronia breaches the Convention — the conduct of its courts is attributable to it (Art 4 ARSIWA); a difference between the UN and Feronia goes to an ICJ advisory opinion, accepted as decisive (Section 30).
Memorise: Section 18(a) = official words and acts · also v. own State (Mazilu 1989, Cumaraswamy 1999) · SG's finding = 'greatest weight', 'most compelling reasons' · in limine litis · waiver by SG (Section 20) · court = State organ (Art 4 ARSIWA) · Section 30 opinion 'decisive'.

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 2(c): The United Nations runs a humanitarian logistics hub, part of the UN Secretariat, in State Feronia, a UN member and party to the 1946 Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the United Nations. Feronian prosecutors are investigating whether managers of the trucking company TransCargo, a former contractor of the hub, bribed customs officials. Without asking the UN, Feronian police want to enter the hub's offices and warehouse and seize its procurement files. Their chief argues: 'The hub is not extraterritorial — it is Feronian territory, so Feronian law and Feronian police powers apply there.' Is the police chief right, and may the police enter? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: He is right that the hub is not extraterritorial, but wrong in his conclusion: UN premises are inviolable and its documents are inviolable wherever located, so the police may neither enter nor seize the files without the UN's consent.
• Not extraterritorial: the premises remain Feronian territory; Feronian law applies there except where the UN's privileges and immunities displace it.
• Inviolability: UN premises are inviolable, and its property and assets are immune from search, requisition, confiscation and any other interference by executive, administrative, judicial or legislative action (Section 3 General Convention; Art 105(1) Charter); its archives and all documents belonging to or held by it are inviolable wherever located (Section 4) — this covers the procurement files.
• Correct route: Feronia must ask the UN, which must cooperate with national authorities to facilitate the proper administration of justice (Section 21) and may consent to the entry or provide the documents. Entry without consent would be an internationally wrongful act of Feronia.
Memorise: inviolable ≠ extraterritorial · Section 3 premises inviolable + property immune from search · Section 4 documents inviolable wherever located · entry only with the UN's consent · Section 21 duty to cooperate.

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 2(d): The United Nations runs a humanitarian logistics hub in State Feronia, a UN member and party to the 1946 Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the United Nations. Its procurement officer Mr Rusk, an ordinary staff member, enjoys immunity only for acts performed in his official capacity. The head of the hub, Ms Okafor, holds the rank of Assistant Secretary-General and is a national of State Ludo. On a private weekend trip in Feronia she causes a traffic accident; the injured cyclist sues her for damages before a Feronian court. Do you agree with the following statement? 'Like Mr Rusk, Ms Okafor is immune only for official acts, so the cyclist can sue her; in any case, only the Security Council could waive her immunity.' Give reasons. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — both parts are wrong: as an Assistant Secretary-General Ms Okafor enjoys diplomatic immunity, which also covers a private traffic accident, and it is the Secretary-General who decides on waiving it; the Security Council waives only the Secretary-General's own immunity.
• Rule: ordinary officials have only functional immunity for official acts (Section 18(a) General Convention); the Secretary-General and all Assistant Secretaries-General (in practice also Under-Secretaries-General) additionally enjoy, for themselves, their spouses and minor children, the privileges and immunities of diplomatic envoys (Section 19).
• Application: a diplomatic agent is immune from civil jurisdiction except for actions on private immovable property, succession matters and professional or commercial activity outside official functions (Art 31(1) VCDR); a private traffic accident is none of these → the court must dismiss the action unless immunity is waived.
• Waiver: the Secretary-General has the right and the duty to waive any official's immunity where it would impede the course of justice and can be waived without prejudice to the UN's interests; the Security Council decides only for the Secretary-General himself (Section 20).
• If immunity is maintained, the UN must provide another mode of settlement for the cyclist's claim (Section 29(b)).
Memorise: staff = Section 18(a) functional · SG + ASG (USG) = Section 19 diplomatic, private acts too (only Art 31(1) VCDR exceptions) · waiver: SG for officials, Security Council for the SG (Section 20) · Section 29(b).

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 3(a): Ruvenia and Talmar are neighbouring States. Mr Kerr, a Talmarian journalist living in Talmar, has published articles accusing Ruvenia's President of corruption. In March 2026 an officer of Ruvenia's intelligence service pays three members of the private motorcycle gang 'Iron Riders' to abduct Kerr and gives them his address, a service car and a detailed plan. The Iron Riders abduct Kerr from his home 40 km inside Talmar and hand him over to the Ruvenian border police, who detain him. Two days later Ruvenia's President declares on television: 'The Iron Riders acted as true patriots. Kerr will remain in Ruvenia until Talmar extradites the opposition leader Vargo, to whom it has granted asylum.' Are the abduction and the continued detention of Kerr attributable to Ruvenia? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes — the abduction is attributable because the Iron Riders acted on the instructions of a Ruvenian State organ (Art 8 ARSIWA), and the detention is conduct of Ruvenia's own organs (Art 4), which the President's declaration moreover acknowledged and adopted as Ruvenia's own (Art 11).
• Basis: a State is responsible for conduct attributable to it that breaches an international obligation (Arts 1–2 ARSIWA); the conduct of private persons as such is not attributable.
• Iron Riders: neither de iure nor de facto organs (no complete dependence on the State, Bosnian Genocide 2007) → not Art 4. But the conduct of persons acting on the instructions of, or under the direction or control of, a State is attributable (Art 8). The intelligence officer, a State organ, ordered and paid for this specific operation and supplied target, car and plan → instructions. Mere financing or support would not suffice (effective control, Nicaragua 1986).
• Detention: the border police are State organs (Art 4) → attributable in any case. 'True patriots' alone would be mere approval, but announcing that Kerr will be held until Talmar extradites Vargo clearly acknowledges and adopts the abduction and detention as Ruvenia's own (Art 11; Tehran Hostages, ICJ 1980).
• Breaches: Talmar's territorial sovereignty (enforcement on foreign territory without consent; cf. the Eichmann abduction, SC Res 138 (1960)) and Kerr's human rights (liberty).
Memorise: private gang → Art 8 instructions (organ ordered the specific operation) · financing or support alone ≠ attribution (Nicaragua, effective control) · police = Art 4 · 'held until …' = acknowledgment and adoption (Art 11, Tehran) · territorial sovereignty (Eichmann).

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 3(b): On the instructions of Ruvenia's intelligence service, Mr Kerr, a Talmarian journalist critical of Ruvenia's President, was abducted from his home in Talmar and handed over to the Ruvenian border police. During the interrogation, two border police officers beat Kerr severely to make him reveal his sources, although the Minister of the Interior had expressly ordered in writing that Kerr be treated correctly. Ruvenia argues that the officers acted against its orders, so their conduct is their own private matter and not Ruvenia's responsibility. Do you agree? Give reasons. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — the conduct of a State organ acting in its official capacity is attributable to the State even if it exceeds its authority or contravenes instructions (Arts 4 and 7 ARSIWA).
• Art 4: the conduct of any State organ, whatever its function or rank, is an act of the State; the border police officers are State organs.
• Art 7: this holds even ultra vires or against instructions, provided the organ acts in that capacity, i.e. under colour of office — as in interrogating a detainee in police custody. Otherwise a State could escape responsibility through internal orders (Youmans 1926; Caire 1929). Only purely private conduct (e.g. an off-duty brawl) is not attributable.
• Breach: a severe beating to extract information is torture (Art 1 Convention against Torture; Art 7 ICCPR; customary law), whose prohibition is ius cogens (Belgium v Senegal, ICJ 2012); internal orders do not change the characterisation under international law (Art 3 ARSIWA). Ruvenia owes reparation and must investigate and prosecute the officers.
Memorise: organ + official capacity → attributable even ultra vires or against orders (Art 7; Youmans, Caire) · private off-duty act ≠ attributable · internal orders no excuse (Art 3) · torture = ius cogens.

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 3(c): A 2019 police cooperation agreement between the neighbouring States Ruvenia and Talmar allows Ruvenian police officers in hot pursuit of a person caught committing a crime to continue the pursuit up to 10 km into Talmar; any person arrested there must be handed over immediately to the Talmarian police. In 2026, on the instructions of a Ruvenian intelligence officer, members of the private motorcycle gang 'Iron Riders' abducted Mr Kerr, a Talmarian journalist critical of Ruvenia's President, from his home 40 km inside Talmar and brought him to Ruvenia, where he is detained. Ruvenia argues that the operation was covered by the consent Talmar gave in the 2019 agreement. Assess. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — consent precludes wrongfulness only to the extent that the act remains within the limits of that consent (Art 20 ARSIWA), and the abduction exceeds every limit of the 2019 agreement.
• Context: consent is one of six circumstances precluding wrongfulness (Arts 20–25: consent, self-defence, countermeasures, force majeure, distress, necessity); none justifies a breach of a peremptory norm (Art 26).
• Art 20: valid consent — freely given by a competent authority, clearly established, given before or at the time of the act — covers only the conduct consented to.
• Application: Talmar consented to hot pursuit by Ruvenian police officers of a person caught committing a crime, up to 10 km into Talmar, with immediate handover to the Talmarian police. Kerr was neither pursued nor caught committing a crime; the abductors were private gang members, not police; they acted 40 km inside Talmar; and Kerr was taken to Ruvenia → outside the consent; Talmar's territorial sovereignty is violated.
• Moreover, consent operates only in relation to the consenting State: Talmar could not waive Kerr's own human rights.
Memorise: six circumstances (Arts 20–25) · consent = valid, competent authority, before or at the time, only within its LIMITS (Art 20) · only vis-à-vis the consenting State · Art 26 ius cogens.

cards.q: Mock exam 1 — Question 3(d): On the instructions of a Ruvenian intelligence officer, members of a private gang abducted Mr Kerr, a Talmarian journalist critical of Ruvenia's President, from his home in Talmar; he is now held by the Ruvenian police. Ruvenia's President declared on television that Kerr 'will remain in Ruvenia until Talmar extradites the opposition leader Vargo', to whom Talmar has granted political asylum. Before acting, Ruvenia never asked Talmar to comply with any obligation. Ruvenia's Foreign Minister now states: 'Even if Ruvenia is responsible, holding Kerr is a lawful countermeasure, because by refusing to extradite Vargo Talmar breaches our bilateral extradition treaty.' Do you agree? Give reasons. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — holding Kerr cannot be a lawful countermeasure: a prior wrongful act of Talmar is doubtful, the procedural conditions were ignored, and above all countermeasures may never affect obligations for the protection of fundamental human rights (Art 50(1)(b) ARSIWA) — detaining a private person as a bargaining chip is hostage-taking.
• Concept: countermeasures (Arts 22, 49–54) are otherwise unlawful measures taken by an injured State against the responsible State in response to its prior wrongful act and to induce it to comply; they consist in the temporary non-performance of obligations owed to that State and must as far as possible be reversible (Art 49).
• Prior wrongful act: extradition treaties usually exclude political offences, and granting asylum is not in itself unlawful; a State taking countermeasures acts at its own risk.
• Conditions: Ruvenia had to call on Talmar to comply, notify its decision and offer to negotiate (Art 52(1)) — it did none of this; the measure must also be commensurate with the injury (Art 51).
• Prohibited (Art 50(1)): threat or use of force, fundamental human rights, humanitarian obligations prohibiting reprisals, other peremptory norms. Holding Kerr until Talmar extradites Vargo violates his right to liberty and is hostage-taking (detaining a person to compel a State to act as a condition for release, Hostages Convention 1979); his rights are not obligations owed only to Talmar.
• Consequences: Ruvenia must cease and release Kerr (Art 30), return him to Talmar (restitution, Art 35), pay compensation (Art 36) and give satisfaction, e.g. an apology (Art 37).
Memorise: countermeasure = prior wrong + against the wrongdoer + to induce compliance + call to comply, notification, offer to negotiate (Art 52) + proportionate (Art 51) + reversible (Art 49) · never: force, human rights, humanitarian reprisals, ius cogens (Art 50) · person as bargaining chip = hostage-taking.
